prompt: An instance is launched with a script in --user-data. What runs that script?
hint: EC2 stores the text; something else acts on it.

choices.text: EC2 itself, before handing the instance over
choices.why: EC2 never reads or runs user data. It stores the text and hands it back when the instance asks.

choices.text: cloud-init, inside the image, on the first boot
choices.why: cloud-init fetches the text from the metadata service early in the first boot and runs it as root.

choices.text: The AWS CLI, after run-instances returns
choices.why: The CLI only base64-encodes the file and sends it. It is finished before the instance boots.

choices.text: The launch template, every time the instance starts
choices.why: A launch template can carry user data, but it runs nothing, and the script does not run at every start.

prompt: first-boot.sh is 395 bytes and its base64 form is 528 characters, four for every three. How many base64 characters does a 3,000-byte script become?
hint: 3,000 divides by 3 exactly, so there is no padding.

prompt: A web server launched with first-boot.sh is rebooted a week later. What does cloud-init do with the user data on that reboot?
hint: It keeps a record of what it has already done for this instance.

choices.text: It runs the script again, so nginx is reinstalled
choices.why: That would be true of a service the script installed, not of the script. cloud-init runs it on the first boot only.

choices.text: It downloads the newest user data and runs that instead
choices.why: Even replaced user data is not run again on a later boot of the same instance.

choices.text: It refuses to boot until the user data is removed
choices.why: Nothing about a reboot depends on the user data; the instance boots normally.

choices.text: Nothing: the instance has had its first boot
choices.why: cloud-init records the first boot and skips user-data scripts after it, which is why the script enables nginx.

prompt: Who can read the user data of an instance in full? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section decoded it with one permission, and named a path on the instance.

choices.text: Anybody allowed ec2:DescribeInstanceAttribute in the account
choices.why: That permission returns the base64, and base64 is an encoding, not encryption.

choices.text: Any process on the instance that can reach the metadata service
choices.why: /latest/user-data answers any process on the instance, not only root.

choices.text: Anybody on the internet who knows the instance's public address
choices.why: 169.254.169.254 is link-local and answers from inside the instance only.

choices.text: Only the account's root user, because the text is encrypted
choices.why: It is stored base64-encoded, which anybody can decode, as the capture did with base64 -d.

prompt: Forty instances in an auto scaling group were launched with a user-data script that installs the wrong version of an agent. What puts the right version on the fleet?
hint: Changing the text on an instance does not re-run a first boot.

choices.text: Stop each instance, replace its user data and start it again
choices.why: AWS allows the replacement while stopped, but cloud-init will not run it, because the first boot is over.

choices.text: Launch replacements from a fixed template version
choices.why: New instances have a first boot, so they run the new script; an instance refresh, from lesson 4, does the replacing.

choices.text: Reboot them all, since the script runs at every boot
choices.why: It runs on the first boot only, so a reboot changes nothing.

choices.text: modify-instance-attribute on the running instances
choices.why: AWS refuses that on a running instance, and moto accepting it proved only that moto does not check.

prompt: Why does a request to the metadata service need no access key and no signature?
hint: Think about what kind of address 169.254.169.254 is.

choices.text: AWS signs it on the instance's behalf at the internet gateway
choices.why: The request never reaches an internet gateway; the host under the instance answers it.

choices.text: The metadata it returns is public anyway
choices.why: It returns role credentials and user data, which are anything but public.

choices.text: Only the instance reaches it, so its origin is the identity
choices.why: The address is link-local and no router forwards it, so a request that arrives came from that instance.

choices.text: The session token replaces the key
choices.why: Even IMDSv1, with no token, needed no key. The token defends against forged requests; it is not an identity.

prompt: From inside an instance, the metadata service is reached at the link-local IPv4 address ___.
hint: Four numbers, two of them repeated.

prompt: moto's metadata path answered us-east-1a for the zone, while every instance the lab launched was in sa-east-1a. What does that answer tell you?
hint: Compare it with the id it gave: i-fake.

choices.text: That moto moved the instance to another Region
choices.why: describe-instances still placed every instance in sa-east-1a; nothing moved.

choices.text: That the region variable is set wrongly in this terminal
choices.why: AWS_DEFAULT_REGION is sa-east-1, and the CLI was not even involved: curl asked moto directly.

choices.text: That the metadata service answers for the account's default Region
choices.why: On AWS it answers for the instance asking; there is no account-wide answer.

choices.text: Nothing about any instance: it is a fixed placeholder
choices.why: moto serves the same answers whatever was launched, for SDKs under test. On AWS each instance gets its own value.

prompt: With no credential variables set, the CLI on an instance finds its keys in the metadata service. Put its requests in order.
hint: The --debug lines showed three requests before the real call.
items: The signed call to the AWS API with those keys
trap: Asking for the role's keys before knowing its name: the name comes from the listing.

prompt: A web application fetches any URL a user pastes. Under IMDSv2, why does pasting the credentials URL no longer return keys?
hint: What does the application send, and what does the service now demand first?

choices.text: The service blocks every request coming from a web server process
choices.why: It cannot tell which process asked, and the CLI on the same instance is answered.

choices.text: The URL changed, so the old path no longer exists
choices.why: The paths are the same in both versions; first-boot.sh reads the same tree.

choices.text: Its GET has no token, and only a PUT with a custom header gets one
choices.why: The forged request is a GET with headers the application chose, so it never has a token to present.

choices.text: The keys are encrypted with the token, so a request without it reads nothing useful
choices.why: The keys are returned in clear to a request with a valid token; the token gates the read, it encrypts nothing.

prompt: The longest lifetime a token PUT may ask for is 21,600 seconds. How many hours is that?
hint: 3,600 seconds to an hour.

prompt: The metadata service refuses a token PUT that carries an X-Forwarded-For header. Which path to the credentials does that close?
hint: Which kind of software adds that header?

choices.text: A misconfigured reverse proxy relaying an outside request
choices.why: A proxy forwards any method but adds X-Forwarded-For, so it announces itself as a relay and is refused.

choices.text: A container on a bridge network
choices.why: The container is stopped by the hop limit, not by a header; it adds no X-Forwarded-For.

choices.text: An old SDK that still speaks IMDSv1
choices.why: An IMDSv1 client sends no PUT at all, so this rule never meets it.

choices.text: A user-data script run as root
choices.why: user data runs on the instance itself and sends no such header; first-boot.sh gets its token.

prompt: A container on a Docker bridge network, on an instance with tokens required and a hop limit of 1, times out asking for credentials. It needs to write to one S3 bucket. What is the better fix?
hint: Raising the limit works; ask what it hands the container.

choices.text: Its own role, with only the permission it needs
choices.why: A task role, lesson 8, gives that container just the permission it needs and leaves the instance's role out of reach.

choices.text: Set HttpTokens back to optional so the container can use IMDSv1
choices.why: That reopens the forged-GET path for every program on the instance to fix one container.

choices.text: Raise the hop limit to 2, which lets it borrow the instance's role
choices.why: It works, and every container on the instance then gets the instance's role, with all of its permissions.

choices.text: Put an access key in the container's environment
choices.why: A static key never expires on its own and is readable by anybody who can inspect the container.

prompt: Match each header or setting to what it does in IMDSv2.
hint: Two travel with the requests, one is refused, one is set on the instance.

pairs.right: How long the requested token lives
The token, presented on every read
Marks a relay, so the token PUT is refused
How many hops the token reply survives

right_distractors: The name of the role the keys belong to

prompt: Tokens are required on an instance. Which of these can still read the role's credentials?
hint: IMDSv2 stops requests somebody tricked a program into making.

choices.text: A forged URL sent through the app's image-fetching feature
choices.why: That is a GET with no token, refused with 401.

choices.text: Code an attacker managed to run on the instance
choices.why: Code that can send its own requests sends the PUT like the CLI does. Least privilege on the role limits what that costs.

choices.text: A container behind a bridge with the hop limit at 1
choices.why: The token reply dies at the bridge, so it never gets a token.

choices.text: A request relayed by a reverse proxy
choices.why: The proxy's X-Forwarded-For gets its token PUT refused.

prompt: An instance shows HttpTokens: optional. A process sends a GET for the credentials with no token at all. What happens on AWS?
hint: optional means both versions are spoken.

choices.text: It is answered, because IMDSv1 still works beside IMDSv2
choices.why: That is why optional protects nothing against a forged GET.

choices.text: It gets 401, since a token is the only way in
choices.why: That is required. With optional, a request with no token is IMDSv1 and is answered.

choices.text: It is answered only if the hop limit is 2
choices.why: The hop limit applies to the token PUT's reply, and this request sent no PUT.

choices.text: The instance is stopped until somebody sets HttpTokens to required
choices.why: Nothing stops an instance over its metadata options.

prompt: Which of these make new instances require tokens without anybody adding --metadata-options to each launch? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look for settings that sit above a single launch.

choices.text: MetadataOptions in the launch template the group uses
choices.why: Every instance launched from that version starts with them.

choices.text: The account default set with modify-instance-metadata-defaults
choices.why: It applies to every launch in that Region that does not name its own options.

choices.text: An AMI registered with --imds-support v2.0
choices.why: Instances launched from it get HttpTokens required, which Amazon Linux 2023's images carry.

choices.text: modify-instance-metadata-options on the instance running today
choices.why: That changes one existing instance; tomorrow's launches are not touched.

choices.text: A hop limit of 2 on the launch template
choices.why: The hop limit says how far a token travels, not whether one is required.

prompt: Before setting required on a fleet, an engineer reads each instance's MetadataNoToken metric. What is she looking for?
hint: The name says what it counts.

choices.text: How many tokens each instance has issued
choices.why: It counts reads without a token, not tokens issued.

choices.text: Programs still reading metadata with IMDSv1, which required would break
choices.why: A metric that has read zero for a couple of weeks means the switch breaks nothing.

choices.text: Failed SSRF attempts against the instance
choices.why: A refused forged request is not what it counts, and with optional nothing is refused.

choices.text: Instances that have no role attached
choices.why: An instance without a role still answers metadata reads, and still counts them.

prompt: An IAM policy can deny ec2:RunInstances unless the condition key ec2:___ equals required.
hint: It is named after the launch setting, prefixed with Metadata.

prompt: moto reported HttpTokens: sometimes and a hop limit of 65 as applied. What would AWS have done?
hint: AWS accepts two values for one and a range for the other.

choices.text: Applied them too; AWS rounds the hop limit down to 64
choices.why: AWS rounds nothing here; values outside the allowed set are refused.

choices.text: Refused both values
choices.why: Tokens are optional or required, and the limit runs from 1 to 64. moto stores what it is given. A script that passes against moto has been checked for shape, not values.

choices.text: Accepted sometimes as a synonym of optional
choices.why: There is no such synonym; the request is invalid.

choices.text: Applied them after a reboot of the instance
choices.why: Valid options apply without a reboot, and these are not valid.

prompt: Put the steps of moving a running fleet to IMDSv2 in a safe order.
hint: Find what would break before breaking it; make it impossible to undo last.
items: Read MetadataNoToken to find who still uses IMDSv1
Update those agents and scripts until the metric stays at zero
Publish a launch template version with tokens required
Replace the instances with an instance refresh
Deny launches without required in a policy
trap: Requiring tokens before the metric reads zero breaks whatever still speaks IMDSv1. The metric comes first, and the policy last, once nothing needs optional.

prompt: A user-data script runs for 20 minutes and reads metadata throughout, with tokens of 300 seconds. What is the fewest tokens it must ask for?
hint: 20 minutes in seconds, over the lifetime of one token.

prompt: A monitoring agent last updated in 2018 stops reporting the moment HttpTokens is set to required. The agent's other features still work. What is the likeliest reason?
hint: When did IMDSv2 appear?

choices.text: It reads the instance's metadata with IMDSv1, which predates it
choices.why: IMDSv2 arrived in November 2019, so an agent from 2018 sends plain GETs, and they now get 401.

choices.text: It runs in a container and the hop limit is 1
choices.why: Nothing says it runs in a container, and the change that broke it was the token, not the limit.

choices.text: Its role lost its permissions when the setting changed
choices.why: Metadata options do not touch IAM; the role's policies are unchanged.

choices.text: The metadata service was turned off
choices.why: That would be HttpEndpoint disabled; required keeps the service on.

prompt: A script launched on thirty instances must write each instance's own Availability Zone into a page. Where should the zone come from?
hint: The same text runs on all thirty.

choices.text: Typed into the user data before each launch
choices.why: Then the group, which launches from one template, writes the same zone on every instance.

choices.text: From AWS_DEFAULT_REGION in the instance's environment
choices.why: That is a Region, not a zone, and nothing sets it on a fresh instance.

choices.text: From describe-instances, called on the instance with the account's access key
choices.why: It works only with a key on the instance, which is the static secret the lesson avoids.

choices.text: From placement/availability-zone in the metadata service, read at boot
choices.why: Each instance asks about itself, so one script is right on all thirty, as first-boot.sh does.
